title: Residential segregation and the fertility of immigrants and their descendants
design_class: observational — hierarchical (multilevel) Poisson log-linear model with random Local-Authority intercepts on linked longitudinal census + birth-register data; no exogenous variation, but childhood community composition is measured before childbearing to remove reverse causation/simultaneity
exposure: childhood community population composition / residential segregation, measured in the 1971 census (before childbearing): (a) size and (b) proportion of foreign-born or same-country-of-birth-group population in the Local Authority, and (c) ward-level index of dissimilarity, each ranked into top 5% / 5-25% / bottom 75% (top 2% / 3-5% / bottom 95% for South Asians)
outcome: completed fertility (total children born to each woman by 2009)
effect_estimate: All migrants (Table 2, IRR vs ancestral natives=1.0): child migrants raised in top-5% most foreign-born LAs IRR 1.14*** (size, Model A1); index-of-dissimilarity top 5% IRR 1.25*** (Model A5, ~25% more children than natives); least-segregated migrants not significantly different from natives. Pakistani/Bangladeshi (Table 3): top-2% size IRR 1.61*** (first gen), 1.57*** (second gen); index of dissimilarity top 40% IRR 1.75***. Indian (Table 4): top-2% size IRR 1.28**. Higher segregation/co-ethnic concentration in childhood -> higher completed fertility (i.e., less exposure to the native low-fertility norm).
effect_se_or_ci: SEs reported. Table 2: A1 top 5% SE 0.03; A5 top 5% SE 0.06. Table 3 (Pak/Bangladeshi): top 2% size SE 0.16 (1st gen), 0.13 (2nd gen); IoD top 40% SE 0.15. Table 4 (Indian): top 2% SE 0.10. Significance stars: *p<.05, **p<.01, ***p<.001.
identifies_diffusion_vs_common_shock: no — no exogenous variation in segregation; it is a multilevel association. The childhood-exposure design removes reverse causation and simultaneity (exposure measured before the woman's own childbearing) but does not separate true socialisation/diffusion from parental residential selection into co-ethnic areas or common cultural shocks; authors concede community composition as norm-exposure is a construct-validity assumption and flag the modifiable areal unit problem.
setting_sample: England & Wales; ONS Longitudinal Study (1% sample) linked 1971-2009; women under 16 in 1971 followed to completed fertility in 2009; N=50,152 (44,168 ancestral natives, 1,074 first-generation child migrants, 4,910 second generation), with a South Asian (Pakistani/Bangladeshi, Indian) focus.
routing_check: confirmed A.3 — Wall-1 residential-segregation paper whose estimand is diffusion of fertility norms: it tests the childhood-socialisation hypothesis, treating segregation as a diffusion-limiting social structure that governs childhood exposure to the native low-fertility norm versus the origin-culture high-fertility norm (‘cultural entrenchment’). This is diffusion-of-fertility-behaviour content, not pure composition, and not a content-agnostic channel (so not A.20).
risk_of_bias: serious — confounding: residual selection from parents sorting into co-ethnic/segregated neighbourhoods on unobserved fertility preferences, plus construct-validity of composition as a proxy for norm exposure and the modifiable areal unit problem; the childhood-timing design is a genuine strength that removes reverse causation but provides no exogenous variation.
notes: All estimates are full-text (Tables 2-4), not abstract-only. Methodologically careful (completed fertility, pre-childbearing exposure, multiple composition measures giving consistent results), and the strongest observational design of the segregation pair, but still unidentified in the diffusion-vs-common-shock sense. Findings support the childhood-socialisation / diffusion reading: fertility of immigrants is closer to native fertility when they grow up in less segregated areas.
